'All is NOT lost!' - Thousands of Burkinabe FLEE Guinea gold-mining crackdown, find REFUGE in Mali

Thousands of Burkinabe nationals expelled from gold-mining sites in Guinea have arrived in Mali, where authorities and youth volunteers are providing shelter and assistance as efforts to organise their return home continue.

Footage filmed in Bamako on Thursday shows Burkinabe nationals queuing with their belongings, boarding trucks and gathering at transport stations as volunteers coordinate assistance.

"We thank the Malian people. They have welcomed us warmly, from the border all the way here to Bamako. They welcomed us and gave us water. We are truly grateful to them," said Burkinabe gold miner Zongo Sylvain.

Local youth groups have mobilised to help the arrivals reach reception centres.

"Yesterday, young people mobilised across all communes. The government took the initiative to involve young people in assisting our Burkinabe brothers who had left Guinea. That is why we mobilised. Since yesterday, the Sogoniko site has been full," said Zakaria Diarra, Chairman of the Commune VI Youth Council.

He urged volunteers to treat the arrivals with compassion.

"Among them, there may be people who will become ministers, and others who will become presidents," he said. "So we must take care of them and encourage them to understand that all is not lost."

More than 8,000 people, mostly Burkinabè nationals, had reportedly arrived at Mali’s Kouremale border crossing by November 2 following Guinea’s crackdown on illegal gold mining in Siguiri.

Malian authorities reported at least four deaths and around 100 people requiring medical treatment, including some with gunshot wounds.
